explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The writer says, "it is fitting for the upright to praise Him." Fitting means it suits them, the way this tall white hat suits me. Rejoicing and praising come in the same breath here.

Not this time, friend. Read the verse again: "Rejoice in the LORD, O righteous ones; it is fitting for the upright to praise Him." So the writer does say it, right there in the first line. Fitting means praise suits the upright, and I'd say that's a pretty warm invitation.

Hold on, baker, this song isn't a library song. The writer says, "play skillfully with a shout of joy." A shout of joy is the opposite of quiet. I'd get loud before the second line, and I don't even own an instrument.
That's right. Verse 3 says, "Sing to Him a new song; play skillfully with a shout of joy." So the harp and ten strings come with a shout. Nobody is told to whisper this one.
Careful, friend, the psalm says the opposite. Verse 4 says, "…all His work is trustworthy." All, not most and not some. I've had plenty of batches I couldn't vouch for, but that's a me problem.
Yes, baker. The writer says the word of the LORD is upright, and "…all His work is trustworthy." There's no fine print and no exceptions in that line. Every bit of it can be trusted.

That's it. Verse 5 says, "the earth is full of His loving devotion." Full, like a cookie box packed to the lid. After hearing that the LORD loves righteousness and justice, this is where the writer lands.

Not quite, friend. The writer says the earth is full of something else: "…His loving devotion." Anger doesn't show up in the verse at all. Right after the LORD's love of righteousness and justice, the verse points to love, not anger.

Close call, baker, but no. The verse says the earth is full of "…His loving devotion." And silence doesn't fit the psalm anyway, since verse 6 and verse 9 are all about what happens when He speaks. This psalm has a lot of noise in it.

You got it, baker. Verse 6 says, "By the word of the LORD the heavens were made, and all the stars by the breath of His mouth." Every star in the sky, and it all came from His breath. Meanwhile I need an oven and a timer to make a single star-shaped cookie.

Good guess, but that one belongs to a different moment: "the LORD God formed the man from the dust of the ground" (Genesis 2:7). For the stars, this psalm says "…the breath of His mouth." Different work, different material. Easy to mix up, baker.
That one's a miss, friend. The psalm never mentions clay or a potter. It says the heavens came by His word, and "…all the stars by the breath of His mouth." No wheel, no kiln, just His breath.

Look at the verse again, friend. It says, "Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the people of the world revere Him." That's all the earth and all the people of the world. The writer's circle is as big as it gets.
That's right. Verse 8 says, "Let all the earth fear the LORD; let all the people of the world revere Him." The writer doesn't narrow it to one people. It's everybody on the earth.

Yes, baker. Verse 10 says, "The LORD frustrates the plans of the nations; He thwarts the devices of the peoples." The writer says it twice, once with each word. I've watched my own plans fall flat, but this is a whole different scale.

Not here, friend. The writer says the LORD "…frustrates the plans of the nations…" A blessing does come up a little later in the psalm, and it's for the nation whose God is the LORD (Psalm 33:12). But in this verse, the nations' plans are frustrated and thwarted.
Close, but no. In the psalm, the LORD doesn't follow the nations' plans. He "frustrates" them and "thwarts" them. His own counsel is the one that stands, as verse 11 says.
That's the word. Verse 11 says, "The counsel of the LORD stands forever…" Plans of the nations come and go, but His doesn't. I'd call that a pretty good contrast.
Interesting guess, baker, but the verse says something bigger. It says the counsel of the LORD stands "forever." It's about how long His counsel lasts, and it doesn't say anything about being alone.
Not quite, friend. Standing aside is what I do when someone else carries the cookie box. The verse says His counsel stands "forever," and that's a lot stronger than stepping out of the way.

explanations.answer: The nation whose God is the LORD
explanations.explanation: Right, baker. Verse 12 says, "Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD, the people He has chosen as His inheritance!" The blessing goes to the nation that belongs to Him. That's the one the writer calls blessed.

explanations.answer: The nation with the largest army
explanations.explanation: Nice try, but the psalm says otherwise. Verse 16 says, "No king is saved by his vast army…" The blessed nation in verse 12 is the one "…whose God is the LORD…" A big army just doesn't make the list.

explanations.answer: The nation with the richest king
explanations.explanation: Not this one, friend. The psalm never calls a nation blessed for its king's riches. It says, "Blessed is the nation whose God is the LORD…" Money doesn't come up in that line at all.
Yes, baker. Verse 13 says, "The LORD looks down from heaven; He sees all the sons of men." All of them, from the top to the very back of the line. Nobody gets lost in the crowd.
Not quite, friend. The verse says He sees "…all the sons of men." Kings come up later in the psalm, and not as the ones He sees alone. His eyes cover everybody.

That's a miss, baker. The psalm doesn't limit it to priests. Verse 13 says He sees "…all the sons of men." and verse 14 adds that He gazes "…on all who inhabit the earth." That's a wide field of view.
Careful, friend, the psalm says the opposite. Verse 15 says, "He shapes the hearts of each; He considers all their works." Considers means He's paying attention. Not a thing is overlooked.
That's right. The verse says He "…considers all their works." So He doesn't ignore what people do. It comes right after He shapes the hearts of each.
Not so fast, baker. Verse 16 says, "No king is saved by his vast army…" So the army doesn't do the saving, no matter how vast it is. I wouldn't trust my mustache to save me either.

Yes, that's what the psalm says. "No king is saved by his vast army; no warrior is delivered by his great strength." A king can have all the soldiers he wants, and it's still not what saves him. The writer says it plainly, and I like how plain it is.

You got it. Verse 17 says, "A horse is a vain hope for salvation; even its great strength cannot save." The horse has great strength, and the writer still says it can't save. Strength just isn't the thing doing the rescuing.
The psalm says the opposite, friend. It calls a horse "…a vain hope for salvation…" And it adds that "even its great strength cannot save." So it's no sure rescue.
Nice image, baker, but it's not in this psalm. Here the writer says, "A horse is a vain hope for salvation…" The horse is strong, and still it cannot save. That's the whole point of the verse.

That's the first blank. Verse 18 says, "Surely the eyes of the LORD are on those who fear Him…" It's the same word the psalm used back in verse 8 when it called all the earth to fear Him. His eyes are on them.

That's the second blank. The verse says, "…on those whose hope is in His loving devotion" Notice where the hope sits: not in armies or horses, but in His loving devotion. The verse before it said armies and horses can't save, and here is where hope belongs.
Not this one, baker. The verse says His eyes are on those who "fear Him," not those who test Him. Testing isn't in the verse. The word that fits the first blank is fear.

Not this one, friend. The verse says His eyes are on those who "fear Him" and whose "…hope is in His loving devotion" Doubt isn't what the psalm has in mind. Hope fits the second blank, and fear fits the first.

That one doesn't fit, baker. The psalm doesn't say His eyes are on those whose anger is in anything. It says those who "fear Him" and those whose "…hope is in His loving devotion" Anger isn't in the verse at all.
That's right. Verse 19 says His eyes are on them "…to deliver them from death and keep them alive in famine." It's a rescue, not a rating. His eyes are on them for the sake of saving them.

explanations.answer: To test their faith in Him
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. The psalm gives the reason, and testing isn't in it. His eyes are on them "…to deliver them from death and keep them alive in famine." I won't add a reason the verse doesn't give.

Good try, baker, but the verse doesn't say that. It says His eyes are on those who hope in His loving devotion "…to deliver them from death and keep them alive in famine." Delivering is the point here, and rewards aren't mentioned.
Yes, baker. Verse 20 says, "He is our help and our shield." Help for when they need a hand, a shield for when they need cover. And all of it happens while their soul is waiting.
Not in this verse, friend. The writer says, "He is our help and our shield." Those are the two names the waiting soul uses here. It's a close-up, personal picture.

That sounds nice, baker, but it isn't what this verse says. Here the writer says the LORD is "…our help and our shield." Picture it like this: help is a hand when you need one, and a shield is cover when trouble comes. That's who He is for the soul that waits.
That's right. Verse 21 says, "For our hearts rejoice in Him, since we trust in His holy name." The rejoicing and the trusting go together. And it circles back to the rejoicing the psalm opened with.

It's true, friend, and the verse says so plainly. "For our hearts rejoice in Him, since we trust in His holy name." The writer gives the trust as the reason for the rejoicing. So this one is a keeper for the true pile.
